summary: A 1978 extension to the SUPDUP protocol that adds graphics support, so a remote host can draw pictures on a user's display. Its status is unknown.

eli5.summary: SUPDUP was good with text screens. This note adds the ability to draw pictures too.

subtitle: Adding graphics to SUPDUP, the remote terminal protocol

tldr.problem: SUPDUP was a powerful protocol for remote text terminals, but programs needed a way to display graphics and drawings over the network without special terminal-dependent software.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 746 extends SUPDUP with a graphics mode that allows programs to send drawing commands (lines, rectangles, text) using a standard command language independent of terminal hardware, with support for coordinate systems, object grouping, and effects like blinking.
tldr.outcome: Programs can now use graphics over SUPDUP with the same simplicity as text, with terminals supporting different levels of graphics capability reporting what they can do.

today: RFC 746 extends SUPDUP with graphics but has never been widely implemented. It represents an early vision of terminal-independent graphics protocols that influenced later work on network graphics systems.

sections.title: Graphics Beyond Text
sections.content: SUPDUP is a remote terminal protocol that was highly effective for text interaction, but network programs needed the ability to display graphics. Rather than require servers to know about every possible terminal type and convert graphics to terminal-specific commands, RFC 746 defines a standard graphics language that terminals can interpret directly. The protocol is designed to be simple for common operations, work across different terminal types (bit matrix displays and display list systems), and handle network loss gracefully without leaving the display in a confused state.
sections.eli5: Instead of teaching the computer about every terminal's graphics capabilities, we teach every terminal one standard graphics language. Then any program can use it.

sections.title: Graphics Commands and Coordinates
sections.content:
Graphics mode is entered with a special code (%TDGRF) and operates with a graphics cursor position distinct from the text cursor. The cursor uses dots (pixels) rather than character positions. RFC 746 supports two coordinate systems: physical coordinates in actual screen dots, and virtual coordinates where the server uses a standard range (±4000 octal) and the terminal scales them to fit the screen.

Drawing commands run from code 100 to 137, with parallel erasing commands from 140 to 177. Terminals report their capabilities via a SMARTS variable that indicates support for features like rectangles (%TQREC), XOR mode (%TQXOR), sets (%TQSET), and blinking (%TQBNK).
sections.eli5: Graphics works with pixel coordinates instead of character positions. The server can ask the terminal 'do you support drawing rectangles?' and the terminal says yes or no. Then the server uses only the features the terminal actually has.

sections.title: Sets, State, and Multiprocessing
sections.content:
Terminals can define up to 200 sets of objects, where each set can be shown, hidden, or moved as a group. This allows multiple processes to draw on the same terminal without interfering: each process can use a different set and clear only its own objects. Input-stream state (cursor position, XOR mode, selected set, coordinate system, and output region) can be saved and restored with %GOPSH commands, allowing processes to safely add their graphics without affecting other programs' displays.

For simple drawing, a program sends a move command, a line command, and repeats. Loss of graphics output does not confuse the terminal because commands contain redundant information—relative addresses are provided for data compression, but absolute coordinates ensure that partial loss of output does not cascade into wrong positions.
sections.eli5: Multiple programs can draw on the same screen by using different 'sets'—like different layers. Each program saves and restores the screen state so nobody interferes with anybody else.

sections.title: Terminal Independence
sections.content:
The protocol accommodates two fundamentally different terminal architectures. Bit matrix terminals store the entire screen as a grid of pixels and support XOR mode (where drawing an object and erasing it are identical) and solid rectangles. Display list terminals store a list of objects to draw and support object-level operations like moving or erasing by manipulating the list. The protocol defines features so that programs can work on all terminals: erasing works on both, sets are optional (non-set terminals can dedicate certain sets to blinking), and rectangles degrade to lines on terminals without rectangle support.

Errors in graphics commands are ignored rather than reported, since the output and input streams are not synchronized. Terminals do their best to follow commands that are possible and continue from there, so missing commands do not cause cascading failures.
sections.eli5: Different screens work differently—some store pixels, others store drawing commands. The graphics language works with both by being flexible about what features are optional.
